title: Sentence Boundaries
kicker: American Diploma · Digital SAT · Standard English Conventions
summary: Find the clauses, test them, and choose the one correct way to join or separate them — comma splices, run-ons, fragments and “however” traps, with 12 practice questions.

blocks.text: What this question type tests

Sentence boundaries belong to the **Standard English Conventions** domain of the Digital SAT Reading and Writing section. This domain is about 26% of the scored questions (11–15 questions across the two modules). The College Board calls the punctuation skill **Boundaries**: it covers punctuation at the end of a sentence and inside a sentence — linking clauses, separating list items, setting off extra information, and knowing when **no** punctuation is needed. This page teaches the first and most important part: where one sentence ends and the next one begins.

On the test you see one short passage (25–150 words) with a blank, like this: “The museum closed at noon ______ the staff began preparing the new exhibit.” The question underneath says: **“Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?”** The four choices look almost the same — the same words with different punctuation (a comma, a semicolon, a period, nothing). Only one choice gives a correct sentence. These questions usually appear in the second half of each module, after the reading questions.

The good news: boundary questions follow a small set of fixed rules. If you learn to find the **clauses** and to test whether each one is **independent**, you can answer almost every one in under a minute — which matters, because you have about 1 minute 11 seconds per question.

blocks.title: الفكرة الأساسية
blocks.text: قبل ما تختار أي علامة ترقيم، اسأل نفسك: الجزء اللي قبل الفراغ جملة كاملة ولا لأ؟ والجزء اللي بعده جملة كاملة ولا لأ؟ لو الاتنين جمل كاملة، يبقى محتاج نقطة أو فاصلة منقوطة (;) أو فاصلة + and/but/so… — الفاصلة لوحدها غلط.
Step 1: Independent vs dependent clauses
A **clause** is a group of words with a subject and a verb. There are two kinds:

rows: Subject + finite verb + a complete thought. It can stand alone as a sentence.
Has a subject and verb, but starts with a word that makes it incomplete. It cannot stand alone.
Because the river flooded the valley …

blocks.text: **Words that make a clause dependent** (subordinating words): although, because, since, when, while, if, unless, until, after, before, whereas, even though, as soon as, so that — and the relative words which, who, whom, whose, that (when they start a describing clause).
**How to test a clause — three quick tests:**

items: **The stand-alone test.** Cover everything else. Read the clause alone with a period at the end. Does it sound like a complete statement? “The river flooded the valley.” ✓ Complete. “Because the river flooded the valley.” ✗ The listener waits for more.

**The finite-verb test.** Find the main verb. Words ending in -ing (flooding), to + verb (to flood) or a past participle on its own (flooded by rain) are NOT finite verbs. “The river flooding the valley.” ✗ No finite verb, so not a sentence.

**The “I realized that …” test.** Put “I realized that” in front of the clause. If the result makes sense, the clause is independent. “I realized that the river flooded the valley” ✓. “I realized that because the river flooded the valley” ✗ — so the “because” clause is dependent.

blocks.title: Find the clauses first
blocks.text: Before you look at the choices, read the full text and mark the two halves around the blank. Ask: “Left side complete? Right side complete?” Your answers to these two questions decide the punctuation almost every time.
Step 2: The 4 correct ways to join two independent clauses
When BOTH sides are independent clauses, you have exactly four correct options. Learn this table — it is the heart of the whole topic.

rows: The bridge was finished in 2010. It carries 50,000 cars a day.
The bridge was finished in 2010; it carries 50,000 cars a day.
The bridge was finished in 2010, and it carries 50,000 cars a day.
Colon (only when the second clause explains the first)
The bridge was a success: it carried 50,000 cars a day in its first year.

blocks.text: **FANBOYS** = for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so. These are the coordinating conjunctions. Only these seven can join two independent clauses with a comma.

**The semicolon's job** (the teacher's rule): a semicolon joins two independent clauses that are closely related. Both sides must be complete sentences — think of a semicolon as a “soft period.” If you could not put a period there, you cannot put a semicolon there.

**The colon's job:** a colon comes after a complete sentence and introduces a list, an explanation, emphasis or extra information. When you use it to join two clauses, the second clause must explain or expand the first.

items: ✓ The bakery's ovens broke down on Friday; the owners gave away free coffee instead of bread.
✓ The bakery's ovens broke down on Friday, so the owners gave away free coffee instead of bread.
✓ The owners had a simple plan: they would give away free coffee until the ovens were fixed. (the second part explains the plan)
✗ The bakery's ovens broke down on Friday, the owners gave away free coffee instead of bread. (comma splice)
✗ The bakery's ovens broke down on Friday the owners gave away free coffee instead of bread. (run-on)
✗ The bakery's ovens broke down on Friday; so the owners gave away free coffee. (semicolon + FANBOYS — use a comma before “so” instead)

blocks.title: Period = semicolon on the SAT
blocks.text: Between two independent clauses, a period and a semicolon are grammatically equal. So the test will never offer both as the only difference between two choices — that would give two correct answers. If you see “. The” and “; the” both looking right, look again: one of them must have a different problem somewhere else.
Step 3: The three big errors
Error 1: The comma splice
A **comma splice** is two independent clauses joined with only a comma. It is the single most common wrong answer in boundary questions.

items: ✗ Camels can drink 100 liters of water in a few minutes, they store energy as fat in their humps.
✓ Camels can drink 100 liters of water in a few minutes; they store energy as fat in their humps.
✓ Camels can drink 100 liters of water in a few minutes. They store energy as fat in their humps.

blocks.text: Watch out for pronouns. A second clause that starts with **it, they, this, these, she, he, which** is often the clue. “This,” “it” and “they” start independent clauses; “which” starts a dependent clause.

items: ✗ The team finished the survey early, this gave them time to check the data.
✓ The team finished the survey early, which gave them time to check the data. (which-clause = dependent, so a comma is fine)

blocks.text: Error 2: The run-on (fused sentence)
A **run-on** is two independent clauses with no punctuation and no joining word between them.

items: ✗ The library opens at nine on weekdays it opens at ten on Saturdays.
✓ The library opens at nine on weekdays, but it opens at ten on Saturdays.

blocks.text: Error 3: The fragment
A **fragment** is a group of words punctuated as a sentence (capital letter + period) that is not a complete sentence. Common causes:

items: **A dependent clause alone:** ✗ Although the results were surprising. ✓ Although the results were surprising, the team repeated the test.
**No finite verb:** ✗ The new stadium, holding more than 70,000 fans. ✓ The new stadium holds more than 70,000 fans.
**A period that cuts off a which-clause:** ✗ The plan saved money. Which pleased the board. ✓ The plan saved money, which pleased the board.

**A subject + extra information but no main verb:** ✗ The researcher, who had studied the desert for ten years and knew every path. ✓ The researcher, who had studied the desert for ten years, knew every path.

blocks.title: The long-subject trick
blocks.text: When a sentence has a long subject with extra information between commas, cross out the extra information. In “The Rosetta Stone, discovered in 1799, gave scholars …” cross out “discovered in 1799.” Now you can see the subject (Rosetta Stone) and check that it has a real verb (gave).
Dependent + independent: how to punctuate

rows: When the storm ended, the fishermen returned to the harbor.
Independent first, then a dependent clause (because, when, if, after…)
The fishermen returned to the harbor when the storm ended.
The storm ended at dawn, which surprised the forecasters.
✗ When the storm ended; the fishermen returned.

blocks.text: Conjunctive adverbs: however, therefore, as a result …

Words like **however, therefore, consequently, moreover, furthermore, nevertheless, meanwhile, thus, instead, otherwise, as a result, in fact, for example, in addition** are NOT FANBOYS. They show a logical link, but they cannot join two independent clauses with a comma. When one of them starts the second independent clause, put a **semicolon or a period before it** and (usually) a **comma after it**.

items: ✗ The road was closed, however, the bus found another route. (comma splice)
✓ The road was closed; however, the bus found another route.
✓ The road was closed. However, the bus found another route.
✓ The road was closed, but the bus found another route. (FANBOYS — comma is enough)

blocks.text: **But** — when the adverb sits in the middle of ONE clause, it is just extra information and takes a pair of commas:

items: ✓ The bus, however, found another route. (one clause only: “The bus found another route.”)
✗ The bus; however, found another route. (the left side “The bus” is not a clause)

blocks.text: **How to decide:** look at what comes before and after “however.” If there is a complete sentence on BOTH sides, you need “; however,” or “. However,”. If “however” interrupts a single sentence, use “, however,”.

blocks.title: however وأخواتها
blocks.text: كلمات زي however / therefore / as a result مش زي and و but. لو قبلها جملة كاملة وبعدها جملة كاملة، لازم قبلها ; أو نقطة، وبعدها فاصلة: ; however, — أما لو جت في نص جملة واحدة يبقى بين فاصلتين: , however,
Question marks: direct questions only

Use a question mark only for a **direct question** — the actual words someone asks. An **indirect question** reports a question inside a statement, so it ends with a period. Words like “asked whether,” “wondered why,” “wanted to know how” are the clue.

items: ✓ Why do some birds migrate at night? (direct question)
✓ The scientist asked why some birds migrate at night. (indirect — it is a statement)
✗ The scientist asked why some birds migrate at night?
✓ The question is simple: why do some birds migrate at night? (the direct question comes after the colon)

blocks.text: Worked examples
**Worked example 1 — comma splice**

Text: Sea turtles spend most of their lives far out in the ocean. Years later, many females return to the same beach where they hatched to lay their own eggs ______ scientists believe the turtles use Earth's magnetic field to find it.
**Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?**

items: A) eggs, scientists
B) eggs; scientists
C) eggs scientists
D) eggs, and, scientists

blocks.text: **Answer: B**

items: A) ✗ Wrong: Both sides are independent clauses (“many females return …” / “scientists believe …”). A comma alone between them is a comma splice.
B) ✓ Correct: A semicolon correctly joins two closely related independent clauses.
C) ✗ Wrong: No punctuation at all between two independent clauses is a run-on.
D) ✗ Wrong: Comma + “and” would be correct, but the extra comma after “and” is wrong — never put a comma straight after a FANBOYS word here.

blocks.text: **Worked example 2 — conjunctive adverb**

Text: A small team of students built a phone app that helps visitors find their way around a large hospital. The first version of the app was slow and confusing ______ the developers rebuilt it from scratch before releasing it to the public.
**Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?**

items: A) , consequently,
B) ; consequently,
C) , consequently
D) consequently

blocks.text: **Answer: B**

items: A) ✗ Wrong: “Consequently” is not a FANBOYS word, so a comma before it creates a comma splice.
B) ✓ Correct: Two independent clauses with a conjunctive adverb: semicolon before it, comma after it. Correct.
C) ✗ Wrong: Same comma-splice problem as A, and it also drops the comma after the adverb.
D) ✗ Wrong: No punctuation before “consequently” fuses the two clauses into a run-on.

blocks.text: **Worked example 3 — fragment (missing finite verb)**
Text: Egypt's rulers wanted to protect farms from both floods and droughts. The Aswan High Dam, completed in 1970 ______ the yearly flooding of the Nile and stores water in Lake Nasser for dry years.
**Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?**

items: A) 1970, controls
B) 1970, controlling
C) 1970 controls
D) 1970, which controls

blocks.text: **Answer: A**

items: A) ✓ Correct: “Completed in 1970” is extra information between a pair of commas. Removing it leaves “The Aswan High Dam controls … and stores …” — a complete sentence with a finite verb.
B) ✗ Wrong: “Controlling” is an -ing form, not a finite verb. The sentence would have no main verb (fragment) — and “and stores” would have nothing to match.
C) ✗ Wrong: The opening comma after “Dam” needs a matching closing comma after “1970.”
D) ✗ Wrong: “Which controls” turns the rest into a dependent clause, so the subject “The Aswan High Dam” never gets a main verb: fragment.

blocks.text: **Worked example 4 — colon for an explanation**

Text: Wildlife researcher Omar Saleh spent two summers following a family of desert foxes. He noticed something unusual about the foxes he studied ______ they were active during the hottest hours of the day, when their prey was easiest to catch.
**Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?**

items: A) studied, they
B) studied: they
C) studied they
D) studied, so that they

blocks.text: **Answer: B**

items: A) ✗ Wrong: Two independent clauses joined by a comma only: comma splice.
B) ✓ Correct: The first clause is complete and says he noticed “something unusual”; the second clause explains what it was. This is exactly the colon's job.
C) ✗ Wrong: No punctuation between two independent clauses: run-on.
D) ✗ Wrong: “So that” means “in order that” (purpose). The foxes were not active in order that he noticed them, so the meaning is illogical.

blocks.title: Classic traps
items: **The comma splice in disguise:** the second clause begins with “it,” “this,” “they” or a name. A comma alone is never enough.
**“However” with commas only:** “…, however, …” between two complete sentences is a comma splice.
**Semicolon before a dependent clause:** “; because,” “; which,” “; although” — the right side is not complete, so the semicolon is wrong.
**Semicolon + FANBOYS:** “; and” or “; but” between two simple clauses — use a comma instead.
**The broken pair of commas:** the subject is followed by extra information that opens with a comma but never closes it, so the verb looks separated or missing.
**The -ing fragment:** an answer that changes the main verb to an -ing form (“controlling,” “being”) leaves the sentence without a finite verb.
**The indirect question with “?”:** “asked whether …?” — a reported question ends with a period.

blocks.title: Fast strategy for test day
items: Read the whole text, then look at the choices: if only the punctuation changes, it is a boundary question.
Split the sentence at the blank. Test the left side and the right side: complete or not?
Both complete → you need a period, a semicolon, comma + FANBOYS, or a colon (if the second explains the first). Cross out every choice with a comma alone or nothing.
One side incomplete → no semicolon and no period; usually a comma or nothing.
If two choices seem equal (“.” vs “;”), find the other difference — the test never has two correct answers.
Do not spend more than about one minute; these are the questions where you can save time for harder reading items.

blocks.text: Practice
Twelve original questions in SAT format. Take your time, then read every explanation — including for the questions you got right.

blocks.title: Sentence Boundaries — Practice Quiz
blocks.intro: 12 questions · untimed. Choose the answer that makes a correct sentence, then check the explanations.

questions.p: Lake Victoria is the largest lake in Africa and an important source of food for millions of people. The Nile perch, a large predatory fish, was introduced into the lake in the 1950s ______ within a few decades, it had changed the lake's food web completely.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: Both sides are independent clauses, and a semicolon joins them correctly. A is a comma splice, B is a run-on, and D is a comma splice with the conjunctive adverb “however” (it also gives an illogical contrast).

questions.p: Visitors to Islamic Cairo often stop to look up at the huge stone entrance of one mosque in particular. Built in the fourteenth century, the Sultan Hassan Mosque ______ one of the largest mosques of its era and a masterpiece of Mamluk architecture.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: The subject “the Sultan Hassan Mosque” needs a finite main verb: “remains.” “Remaining” and “having remained” are not finite verbs, and “which remains” makes a dependent clause, so B, C and D all leave the sentence as a fragment.

questions.p: A small neighborhood bakery in Alexandria has served fresh bread every morning for more than forty years. Last Friday, however, its two ovens broke down before sunrise ______ the owners gave away free tea and coffee to their regular customers instead.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: Two independent clauses are linked by the conjunctive adverb “therefore,” so it needs a semicolon before it and a comma after it. A and B are comma splices; C has no punctuation at all, making a run-on.

questions.p: Many farmers in South America grow coffee on small family plots. In her lecture, the economist wondered whether small coffee farmers could ever compete with large plantations ______ research suggests that farmers who join cooperatives may have the best chance.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: “Wondered whether …” is an indirect question, so the first sentence is a statement and ends with a period. A wrongly uses a question mark; C is a comma splice; D is a run-on.

questions.p: For years, geologists described the volcano near the village as dormant, meaning that it showed no signs of activity. A new study changed that view. The team's finding surprised everyone ______ the “dormant” volcano had been releasing gas for over a decade.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: The first clause is complete, and the second clause explains the surprising finding, so a colon is correct. A is a comma splice and C is a run-on. D (“because of the volcano had been …”) is ungrammatical: “because of” must be followed by a noun phrase, not a clause.

questions.p: Humans see only part of the light that comes from the sun, but some animals see more. Honeybees, for example, can see ultraviolet light ______ many flowers have ultraviolet patterns on their petals that guide bees toward nectar.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: Two independent clauses can be joined by a comma + FANBOYS (“, and”). A is a comma splice, B is a run-on, and C puts the comma in the wrong place (after “and” instead of before it).

questions.p: Publishers do not always recognize a good book when they see one. Although the novel was rejected by eleven different publishers ______ it later sold millions of copies and was translated into more than forty languages.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: “Although the novel was rejected …” is a dependent clause. A dependent clause at the start of a sentence is followed by a comma. B, C and D all treat the dependent clause as if it were a complete sentence: the semicolon and colon are wrong, and the period leaves a fragment.

questions.p: The ancient city of Petra in southern Jordan was built by the Nabataeans more than two thousand years ago. Many of its tombs and temples were carved directly into rose-colored sandstone cliffs ______ is why travelers often call Petra the Rose City.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: “Which is why …” is a dependent clause that comments on the whole first clause, so it follows a comma. A makes a fragment that begins with “Which”; B puts a semicolon before a dependent clause; D creates a comma splice, because “this is why travelers often call Petra the Rose City” is an independent clause.

questions.p: Solar panels are now common on rooftops around the world, but this was not always the case. The first solar cells of the 1950s were extremely expensive to produce ______ they were used mainly on satellites, where reliability mattered more than cost.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: “As a result” is a conjunctive adverb phrase between two independent clauses, so it needs a semicolon (or period) before it and a comma after it. A and C are comma splices; B is a run-on.

questions.p: For centuries, no one could read the ancient Egyptian hieroglyphs carved on temple walls. The Rosetta Stone, discovered in 1799 by French soldiers near the town of Rashid ______ scholars the key to reading these symbols because it carried the same text in three scripts.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: “Discovered … near the town of Rashid” is extra information, opened by a comma after “Stone” and closed by a comma after “Rashid.” The subject “The Rosetta Stone” then needs the finite verb “gave.” A and C leave the sentence with no main verb (fragment); D is missing the closing comma of the pair.

questions.p: Some of the most important discoveries in science happened by accident. In 1928, Alexander Fleming noticed that mold had killed the bacteria growing in one of his laboratory dishes ______ chance discovery led to the development of penicillin, the first widely used antibiotic.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: “This chance discovery led to …” is an independent clause, so it must be separated from the first independent clause by a period (or semicolon). A and D are comma splices (D also adds a wrong comma after “this”); B is a run-on.

questions.p: The museum in Luxor reopened last month after a long renovation. According to its director, the museum's new exhibit has one clear goal ______ show visitors how ordinary farmers, builders, and families lived in ancient Egypt.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: The first part is a complete sentence, and what follows explains the goal, so a colon is correct. B uses a semicolon before a phrase that is not a clause; C turns “To show visitors …” into a fragment; D is a comma splice.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Test both sides of the blank: is each one an independent clause (subject + finite verb + complete thought)?
Two independent clauses: period, semicolon, comma + FANBOYS, or a colon if the second explains the first. Never a comma alone, never nothing.
however / therefore / as a result between two sentences: “; however,” or “. However,” — inside one sentence: “, however,”.
A dependent clause cannot stand alone and cannot sit next to a semicolon.
Question mark for direct questions only; “asked whether …” ends with a period.
